explanation.value: Process directories bottom-up. For each directory compute three facts about its subtree: the minimum cost, how many files it contains, and whether all of them are flagged (clean). Start from the direct files (each flagged file costs 1 on its own; any unflagged file makes the subtree unclean), add the children's costs and file counts, and combine their clean flags. If the subtree has at least one file and is clean, one directory operation replaces everything, so the cost becomes 1. Otherwise a directory operation is forbidden and the cost is the sum. The root's cost is the answer. The traversal is done iteratively (an explicit stack produces a pre-order list that is processed in reverse) so depth 200 trees do not risk recursion limits.

explanation.value: A directory operation encrypts every file below it, so it is legal only if every one of those files is flagged. When it is legal and the subtree contains at least one file, it covers everything with one operation, which can never be beaten. When it is illegal, the directory's flagged files and subtrees must be handled separately, and those parts are independent.
